docs.title: Cable Connection
docs.text:
Diagram — Cable Connection Schematic   /   Drawning with draw.io   /   Sketches by Vecteezy: Ethernet Cable Vectors, USB Port Vectors

Attention

Put the device somewhere it can stay cool. Keep it away from direct sunlight and heavy dust.

docs.title: Step 1 - Prepare for Network Connection
docs.text:
Use the Ethernet cable to connect your device to your router, as shown in the diagram.

If the provided Ethernet cable isn't long enough, feel free to use another one. Any certified Ethernet cable will work, as long as it's functioning properly.

docs.title: Step 2 - Power Up the Device
docs.text:
Use the USB Type-C cable to connect your device to your power supply, as shown in the diagram.

Please Note

  • Only the RIGHTMOST USB Type-C port is for power input. Don’t mix it up!
  • If you're using your own power supply, make sure it provides a stable 5V and is capable of delivering up to 2A of current. This device doesn’t draw much, only around 2W, but a poor-quality power supply can still make it die young.
  • Do not attempt to power the device via your router’s USB port, unless you're absolutely sure it can provide a stable 5V and up to 2A of current.

Once powered on, the LED will light up. After a few seconds, it will begin blinking.

Now your hardware is ready.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If you run into problems, for example, if the LED doesn't light up at all, or stays solid without blinking.

  • You can try the following steps:

    1. Unplug the USB Type-C power cable.
    2. Double-check that your power supply meets the requirements mentioned above.
    3. Plug the USB Type-C cable into the RIGHTMOST USB Type-C port firmly.

  • If that doesn’t resolve the issue, you can try this additional step:

    1. Unplug the USB Type-C power cable.
    2. Turn your device over and carefully remove and reinsert the microSD card.
    3. Double-check that your power supply meets the requirements mentioned above.
    4. Plug the USB Type-C power cable back in.
  • Or Contact Me for help and support.

docs.title: Use a Proper Device
docs.text: If you're reading this guide on a mobile device, it's better to switch to a laptop or desktop. Some of the upcoming steps may not be supported on mobile platforms.

docs.title: A Reminder
docs.text:
In the next steps you may or may not see the warning similar to one of the cases below. If you do, don't worry. It’s completely normal in this context. It happens because all YANAP services run within your local network, and therefore cannot obtain HTTPS certificates valid for the public internet.

But if you see a similar warning elsewhere, you should be cautious, it could be very dangerous. Always make sure it’s safe before proceeding.

Case 1 (most cases)Case 2 (https typed instead of http)

Click the button in the lower-left corner labeled "Continue to site".

Setp 1 - Click the button in the lower-left corner labeled "Advanced".

Setp 2 - Click the link on the last line that says "Procced to .......... (unsafe)".

docs.title: Keep Device Info Page Ready
docs.text:
Enter the URL below in your web browser to open your Device Info Page.

  • http://yanap.local

You should see a page showing the following information. Keep it open. You’ll need this information in the next steps.

  • Your DNS Server Address
  • Your Router’s Web Interface
  • Your AdGuard Home Web Interface

Note

  • If this page isn't ready or you see "___.___.___.___" (blank, without number) on it, it means the initialization tasks are still running. Please wait a few seconds.
  • The initialization should not take longer than 10 minutes. If you have waited more than 10 minutes, please restart the device and try again.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If you're unable to open http://yanap.local, try using a different web browser or operating system. Some systems or browsers do not support the .local domain.

WindowsmacOS & iOSAndroidLinux
  • Windows 10, Windows 11 support the .local domain by default.
  • Versions prior to Windows 10 do not support the .local domain by default.
  • macOS versions since macOS X Jaguar (version 10.2, 2002) support the .local domain by default.
  • All versions of iOS support the .local domain at the system level, though actual support may vary by app.
  • Android does not support the .local domain out of the box.

  • Most Linux distributions support .local domain, but functionality depends on your specific network configuration.

    Tip

    If you need help enabling support for the .local domain on your Linux distribution, try searching for "mDns configuration for Linux."

docs.title: Default Internet Access Flow
docs.text:
If you have never touched your DNS configuration in your LAN environment, then your situation is similar to the diagram below.

Think of DNS like the internet's address book. When you do anything online, the first step is your device asking a DNS server where to go.

Diagram 1 — Illustrative sketch of the internet access flow with default DNS   /   Drawing with Excalidraw.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

graph LR
  A[Your PC, Phone, Smart TV/Speakers/Plugs, Camera, etc.] -->|➊ send **URL** to| B[DNS Server];
  B -->|➋ reply with matching **IP** to| A;
  A -->|➌ use **IP** to connect to| C[Content / App Servers];
Diagram 2 — Flowchart of the internet access flow with default DNS

"Default" — In other words, you are using the DNS picked by your ISP to serve Their Own Interests.This can lead to the following potential1 consequences:

  • They, your ISP and the DNS service provider, have your metadata — for example, when you go online, and which websites, services, or apps you use. They can't see the full content, but even without that, the metadata alone is usually enough to reconstruct your activity: whether you were watching videos, reading posts, browsing images, or playing games.
  • Often, they sell your metadata to data brokers, ad networks, or other third parties. That's when things get more invasive. Once it's combined with other data sources, they can often figure out exactly what video you watched, which product you checked out, whose profile you viewed, what you searched — all of it. With enough data, you can be identified through profiling and social engineering.
  • Even if your ISP doesn't sell your data, there's still a risk it could be leaked or misused. This could happen through a data breach, careless employees, or government access.
  • In the worst-case scenario, if the DNS server itself is doing evil things, your online safety is seriously at risk. You could be silently redirected to phishing sites, malware, or scams without even realizing it.

These points don't cover every possible risk, but they do show some common ones.

docs.title: Internet Access Flow with DNS-Based Blocker
docs.text:
The AdGuard Home I'm using in YANAP is not the only DNS-based blocker out there. There are other FOSS options that offer similar features, such as Pi-Hole, Technitium, and others. With these DNS filters or blockers, your internet access work like the diagrams 3 and 4.

Diagram 3 — Illustrative sketch of the internet access flow with DNS-Based Blocker   /   Drawing with Excalidraw.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

graph LR
  A[Your Devices] -->|➊ send **URL** to| B[DNS Server];
  B --> |check Blocklist| D{Blocked?};
  D --> |No ➋ send **IP** to| A;
  D --> |Yes ➋ send **0.0.0.0 - Not Found** to| A;
  A --> C{Got Real IP?};
  C -->|Yes ➌ connect to| E[Content / App Servers];
  C -->|No ➌ drop into| F[BlackHole];
Diagram 4 — Flowchart of the internet access flow with DNS-Based Blocker

In this way, you regain all some control over your internet traffic.

docs.title: Can & Can't
docs.text:
A DNS-based blocker isn't a silver bullet, but it's definitely a solid start.

  • Can Block

    # most _____ on websites and apps

    • ads, affiliate
    • tracker, bug tracker, telemetry, metrics
    • Malware, Cryptojacking, scam, spam, phishing
    • social media widgets, in-page pop-ups, other annoyances
    • fake stores, fake streaming, rip-offs
    • native broadband tracker
    • badware hoster
    • malicious scripts
    • adult content
    • gambling content

    # any website you want

    # an entire online service2

  • Can't Block

    # _____ disguised as normal content3

    • video ads on Youtube, Instagram, etc.
    • sponsored posts and ads inside Facebook, TikTok, etc.

    # _____ that doesn’t access internet

    • built-in offline app ads
    • intranet-initiated attacks

    # _____ that doesn’t use your DNS

    • content with fixed IPs
    • content with fixed DNS

    # in-page or in-app scripts, like _____

    • push notifications
    • location requests

  1. Just because I use the word "potential" does not mean that I am unsure of what I am talking about. It's just that ordinary users don't have access to their data centers or logs to audit and expose their actions. ↩

  2. Blocking an entire online service means cutting off all network access related to that service provider. For example, you can block everything from Facebook, TikTok, Amazon, Xbox Live, WeChat, or Twitter. This feature covers categories such as social media, online shopping, video streaming, gambling, online gaming, and more. ↩

  3. Imagine an advertisement printed on tear-proof paper and glued between the regular pages of a dictionary. From the outside, it would be impossible to tell that the dictionary contains ads. You won't know where the ads are until you turn to the page with the ad. And even if you find one, you won't be able to tear it out with your bare hands. ↩

docs.title: Welcome to YANAP!
docs.text:
TL;DR too lang; please read    ¯\(ツ)/¯

YANAP is a combined hardware and software solution that blocks ads, tracking, phishing, and malware in home and small business LAN (Local Area Network) environments.

YANAP stands for "You Are Not A Product".

The intention behind YANAP is to offer a remarkably simple solution for those without an IT background or the spare time to deal with technical complexity, helping them to easily eliminate as many of the intrusive and harmful aspects of the Internet as possible. At its core, the project aims to empower people to reclaim their digital rights and protect their privacy, security, and identity from misuse and abuse.

docs.title: Composition of YANAP
docs.text: Drawing with Excalidraw.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Hardware - SBC (Single Board Computer)
docs.text: I'm using the Radxa Zero 3E as the hardware for YANAP. It's a budget-friendly SBC with enough power to run YANAP smoothly.

docs.title: Software - Thanks to FOSS (Free and Open Source Software)
docs.text:
YANAP is built on four key FOSS projects: DietPi, AdGuard Home, Docker & Docker Compose, and MkDocs Material, and many Contributors who maintain the Filters.

These are the real core components of YANAP. What I’ve done is simply create some lightweight scripts1 to make them self-configuring and self-maintaining, so they can better adapt to your LAN environment.

docs.title: DietPi
docs.text:
a lightweight and highly optimized Debian-based Linux operating system, designed for single-board computers (SBCs) and low-resource devices. It enables this project to run on minimal SBC hardware stably with only a few small tweaks. For you, the user, hat means you won't need to spend a lot of money.

  • Official Website, Official GitHub Repository
  • DietPi is released under the GNU General Public License v2.0 (GPLv2).
  • © 2025 DietPi Contributors

docs.title: Docker & Docker Compose
docs.text:
used in YANAP to provide a stable and isolated runtime environment for AdGuard Home and MkDocs Material, enabling easy deployment and reliable operation.

  • Docker: Official Website, Official GitHub Repository
  • Docker Compose: Official Document of Docker Compose, Official GitHub Repository
  • Docker & Docker Compose are released under Apache License 2.0.
  • © 2025 Docker Inc. All rights reserved

docs.title: AdGuard Home
docs.text:
a network-wide software that gives you control over blocking Advertisement, Tracking, Phishing, Malware, and Adult Content.

  • Official Website, Official GitHub Repository
  • AdGuard Home is released under GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPLv3).
  • © 2009–2025 Adguard Software Ltd.

docs.title: MkDocs Material
docs.text:
a modern, responsive theme for MkDocs, a static site generator. What you’re reading now was built using MkDocs Material.

  • Official Website, Official GitHub Repository
  • MkDocs Material is released under MIT License
  • © 2016–2025 Martin Donath

Acknowledgment

This project would not be possible without the incredible work of the open source community. I express my sincere gratitude not only to the specific projects used in YANAP, but also to all developers, maintainers, document writers, testers, designers, and supporters who contribute to open source software around the world.

Even the tiniest contribution counts!

I encourage everyone to give more attention to open source communities and support them in any way possible:

  • Sharing and Promoting FOSS
  • Providing Feedback and Suggestions
  • Reporting Issues or Bugs
  • Sponsoring or Donating
  • Translating Projects
  • Helping Others in Forums or Discussions
  • Creating Tutorials or How-To Guides
  • Contributing Code

  1. Once I've finished the tests and organized all the scripts and documents, I will also open source my scripts. I will provide an overview after I release the source. ↩

docs.title: Where Your Money Goes
docs.text: This project isn't about making money. I'm doing my best to be as transparent as possible with the costs and keep your price as low as I can.

docs.title: Pricing Logic
docs.text:
Here's the thinking behind the price:

  1. Cover the basics -- hardware and all the direct costs.
  2. Prepare for possible extra costs -- for example, tax-related expenses (if they come up), or the cost of acquiring, maintaining, or replacing the test units I use for development and debugging.
  3. Experiment a little -- give me room to try new ideas for improvements.
  4. Give back -- to support the FOSS that this project relies on, a portion of the money will be donated to them. (More details on how this is done will be shared after the project has been running for a while and once there's a clearer picture of actual ongoing costs.)

docs.title: A Few Notes
docs.text:
• Platform fees aren't included in the prices above. It depends on which platform you choose.
  • Prices may go up or down depending on the hardware market. I'll make adjustments as fairly as I can.

  • MicroSD cards and 3D printed cases are consumables. Their lifespan depends heavily on how and where they're used. In normal conditions, they'll usually last for a few years. But in more extreme environments (like in very hot or sunny places), they might fail much sooner - even within a few months. To give them the best chance, I've chosen endurance-grade cards and sturdy printing materials, balancing durability and cost.

    As long as you use it in the proper environment, there's no need to be overly concerned. Even if they break, the replacement costs are not too expensive.

  • Since the price is already set as close to the actual cost as possible, I'm not able to cover shipping if you ever need to return or replace something. That's one of the trade-offs for keeping things affordable.

docs.title: I Won't Run Any Ads.
docs.text:
• First, ads cost money, and that cost is passed on to you.
  • More importantly, showing ads would go directly against what YANAP is for. It wouldn't make sense to do the opposite just to fund it.

Tip

If you think YANAP is worth using, the best support you can give is simply telling someone else about it. That could be your family, a friend, someone you work or study with, or anyone who might find it useful.

docs.title: Blocking a Service
docs.text:
If you want, AdGuard Home can block an entire online service. This feature is very useful in many situations. For example:

  • Blocking social media in your office.

  • Blocking online gaming platforms when your kids have an online class.

  • When you want to reduce online shopping.

  • Blocking specific companies from snooping around in your data and information.

To do this, click Filters➊, then click Blocked services➋ to open the configuration page.

Click the image to enlarge.

On the configuration page, select the service you want to block and toggle it's switch to On➊.

After that, scroll down in this section and click the Save➋ button to apply the changes.

The service shown in the screenshot is for illustrative purposes only.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

For further precise control you can set up and manage a blocking schedule in the Pause service blocking➌ section below.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Dashboard page provides an overview of your internet requests.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Detail
docs.text:
The Query Log page shows detailed logs of all your internet requests.

Here, you can manually unblock Misblocking or block Missed Block. You’ll learn how to do both on the next page.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Parental Control
docs.text:
If needed, AdGuard Home can block adult content.

To enable this feature, click Settings➊, then click General settings➋ to open the configuration page.

Click the image to enlarge.

On the configuration page, you can activate the Options➊➋ based on your needs.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Temporarily Pause
docs.text:
If you want to temporarily pause blocking, click the dropdown arrow on the Disable protection➊ button and choose a duration.

Or, click the Disable protection➊ button directly to pause indefinitely. You'll need to click it again to manually resume protection.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Sign In
docs.text:
Click the link of Your AdGuard Home Web Interface➊ on Device Info Page to open Your AdGuard Home➋.

Then enter your Username & Password➌ to Sign In➍.

Your Account Information is printed on the paper that came with your package.

Click the image to enlarge.

Note

If you’re manually entering the IP address or URL of Your AdGuard Home Web Interface in the browser, don’t forget to include the port number :7373 at the end.

docs.title: Misblocking
docs.text:
Navigate to Query Log page. Find the URL➊ that you don’t want to block. Click the Three Dots Icon➋ to open the menu, then click Unblock➌.

The unblock takes effect after the system or app clears its DNS cache. This might take just a few seconds, or it could take several minutes depending on the system and application.

The domain shown in the screenshot is for illustrative purposes only.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Missed Block
docs.text:
Navigate to Query Log page. Find the URL➊ that you want to block. Click the Three Dots Icon➋ to open the menu, then click Block➌.

The block takes effect immediately.

The domain shown in the screenshot is for illustrative purposes only.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: ASUS
docs.text:
The set values (e.g., IP address) shown in the screenshots are for reference only. Please follow the tutorial and enter the information shown on your own YANAP page.

The interface on your router may look slightly different depending on your hardware model and firmware version, but the overall process remains the same.

Tip

Don’t worry about messing things up. You can always write down the original values in Step 3. If something goes wrong, just change them back and reboot your router. Everything will work again.

docs.title: Step 1 - Log In to Your ASUS Router
docs.text:
Click the link of Your Router's Web Interface➊ on Device Info Page to open Your Router's Settings Page➋. Enter your Username & Password➌ and click Sign In➍.

  • If you don’t know the password, check the label on your router for the default password.

  • If you’ve changed the default password but forgot it, the only option is to reset your router.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 2 - Find the Setting Page
docs.text:
Once logged in, you will see a page similar to the screenshot below, click LAN➊ from the left sidebar.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 3 - Configure Your DNS Server
docs.text:
On this screen, follow these steps:

  1. Open the DNS configuration panel:

    • click DHCP Server➊

  2. Set your own DNS server addresses:

    • enter IP Address of your DNSv4 server➋ into DNS Server 1➌

    • enter IP Address of your DNSv6 server➍ into IPv6 DNS Server➎

      (If you don’t see IPv6 DNS Server, just skip this step.)

  3. Switch Off This Option:

    • ensure Advertise router's IP in addition to user-specified DNS is set to No➏

  4. Apply the changes:

    • click Apply➐

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 4 - Reboot Your Router
docs.text: Reboot your ASUS router to make sure the changes take effect.

docs.title: Step 5 - Reconnect Your Devices<sup>1</sup>
docs.text:
To make sure everything works right away, you need to reconnect your devices to the internet.

  • If your device connects to the internet via Wi-Fi: Turn Wi-Fi Off then Turn Wi-Fi On.
  • If your device connects to the internet using an Ethernet cable: Unplug the Ethernet Cable then Plug in the Ethernet Cable.
  • If your device connects to the internet via Wi-Fi but has no option to Turn Wi-Fi off / Turn Wi-Fi On: Just restart the device.

docs.title: Done - Test & Move On
docs.text:
From now on, you should see significantly fewer ads, trackers, and pop-ups. Try visiting an ad-heavy website to check if the blocking are working.

All set? Great - now head to Manage Blocking.

  1. This step is optional, but recommended. Some devices don’t refresh their settings automatically after a router reboot, so reconnecting helps ensure everything works as expected. ↩

docs.title: Step 3 - Configure Your DNS Server

docs.title: General Tutorial
docs.text:
Tip

  • Don’t worry about messing things up. You can always write down the original values in Step 4. If something goes wrong, just change them back and reboot your router. Everything will work again.
  • Another tip: You can refer to the tutorials from the "OK List". The interface will look different, and the steps will vary, but the logic and principles are the same.

docs.title: Step 1 - Log In to Your Router
docs.text:
Click the link of Your Router's Web Interface➊ on your Device Info Page to open the settings page of your router.

Then you will be asked to log in.

  • If you don’t know the password, check the label on your router for the default password.

  • If you’ve changed the default password but forgot it, the only option is to reset your router.

docs.title: Step 2 - Find the Setting Page
docs.text:
Find where to change DNS Server on your router's web interface.

  • If you have no idea where to find it, try searching online using this format: Your Router Model/Brand + How to change the DNS server.

docs.title: Step 3 - Configure Your DNS Server
docs.text:
At this step, do one of the following, depending on what your router allows:

  • Option 1

    If there’s a toggle or dropdown like Connect DNS server automatically / Get from ISP / Obtain DNS automatically (or similar wording),

    then switch it to Manual / No / Use the following DNS addresses (or similar wording).

  • Option 2

    If there’s no such toggle, but you see fields already filled with DNS addresses, then delete the existing addresses to clear them out.

Do this for both IPv4 and IPv6 (if IPv6 DNS settings are available).

Note Well: How do I know if IPv6 DNS setting is available or not on my router?

  • Case 1

    If you only see settings labeled IPv4 orDNSv4, and nothing about IPv6 or DNSv6, then ignore all IPv6-related steps.

  • Case 2

    If there are only two blank fields for DNS input, it likely means you can only set IPv4 DNS.

  • Case 3

    If the DNS setting fields only accept numbers (no ":" characters allowed), it means only IPv4 DNS is supported.

docs.title: Step 4 - Enter Your Own DNS Server Address
docs.text:
Now enter your own DNS Server Address shown on Device Info Page.

IPv4 DNS SettingIPv6 DNS Setting
  • Enter IP Address of your DNSv4 server➊ into the first blank field, often labeled Primary DNS, DNS Server 1 or similar wording.
  • Click Save or Apply.
  • If you're unable to save with some fields left blank, try entering the IP Address of your DNSv4 server➊ in all available fields, then click Save or Apply again.
  • Enter IP Address of your DNSv6 server➋ into all blank fields.
  • Click Save or Apply.

docs.title: Step 5 - Reboot Your Router<sup>1</sup>
docs.text: Reboot your router to make sure the changes take effect.

  • If your device connects to the internet using an Ethernet cable: Unplug the Ethernet Cable then Plug in the Ethernet Cable.
  • If your device connects to the internet via Wi-Fi but has no option to Turn Wi-Fi off / Turn Wi-Fi On: Just restart the device.

docs.text:
From now on, you should see significantly fewer ads, trackers, and pop-ups. Try visiting an ad-heavy website to check if the blocking are working.

All set? Great - now head to Manage Blocking.

If you have successfully configured your router by following this General Tutorial.

docs.title: Long Story Short
docs.text:
In this step, you need to replace the default DNS Server Address (usually assigned by your ISP) with your own DNS Server Address displayed on your Device Info Page.

If you know how to handle it, you can skip this part.

docs.title: Short Story Long
docs.text:
I categorize router brands into two groups. One is called the "OK List", and the other is called the "Bad List". The differences are as follows:

  • For every brand on the "OK List", I’ve created a dedicated step-by-step tutorial with screenshots tailored to that brand to walk you through the process.

  • The routers on the "Bad List" have had their features heavily crippled or locked down by the ISP or manufacturer. Gaining full control over your own network on these devices is either impossible or painfully complicated.

    For these cases, I’ve prepared a more involved tutorial compared to the "OK List" routers. It’s still very doable, just requires more patience.

Find your router on one of the two lists, then follow the corresponding tutorial.

If your router is not listed on either list, follow the instructions for "Routers Not on Any List".

docs.title: Cable Connection
docs.text:
Diagram — Cable Connection Schematic   /   Drawning with draw.io   /   Sketches by Vecteezy: Ethernet Cable Vectors, USB Port Vectors

Attention

Put the device somewhere it can stay cool. Keep it away from direct sunlight and heavy dust.

docs.title: Step 1 - Prepare for Network Connection
docs.text:
Use the Ethernet cable to connect your device to your router, as shown in the diagram.

If the provided Ethernet cable isn't long enough, feel free to use another one. Any certified Ethernet cable will work, as long as it's functioning properly.

docs.title: Step 2 - Power Up the Device
docs.text:
Use the USB Type-C cable to connect your device to your power supply, as shown in the diagram.

Please Note

  • Only the RIGHTMOST USB Type-C port is for power input. Don’t mix it up!
  • If you're using your own power supply, make sure it provides a stable 5V and is capable of delivering up to 2A of current. This device doesn’t draw much, only around 2W, but a poor-quality power supply can still make it die young.
  • Do not attempt to power the device via your router’s USB port, unless you're absolutely sure it can provide a stable 5V and up to 2A of current.

Once powered on, the LED will light up. After a few seconds, it will begin blinking.

Now your hardware is ready.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If you run into problems, for example, if the LED doesn't light up at all, or stays solid without blinking.

  • You can try the following steps:

    1. Unplug the USB Type-C power cable.
    2. Double-check that your power supply meets the requirements mentioned above.
    3. Plug the USB Type-C cable into the RIGHTMOST USB Type-C port firmly.

  • If that doesn’t resolve the issue, you can try this additional step:

    1. Unplug the USB Type-C power cable.
    2. Turn your device over and carefully remove and reinsert the microSD card.
    3. Double-check that your power supply meets the requirements mentioned above.
    4. Plug the USB Type-C power cable back in.
  • Or Contact Me for help and support.

docs.title: Use a Proper Device
docs.text: If you're reading this guide on a mobile device, it's better to switch to a laptop or desktop. Some of the upcoming steps may not be supported on mobile platforms.

docs.title: A Reminder
docs.text:
In the next steps you may or may not see the warning similar to one of the cases below. If you do, don't worry. It’s completely normal in this context. It happens because all YANAP services run within your local network, and therefore cannot obtain HTTPS certificates valid for the public internet.

But if you see a similar warning elsewhere, you should be cautious, it could be very dangerous. Always make sure it’s safe before proceeding.

Case 1 (most cases)Case 2 (https typed instead of http)

Click the button in the lower-left corner labeled "Continue to site".

Setp 1 - Click the button in the lower-left corner labeled "Advanced".

Setp 2 - Click the link on the last line that says "Procced to .......... (unsafe)".

docs.title: Keep Device Info Page Ready
docs.text:
Enter the URL below in your web browser to open your Device Info Page.

  • http://yanap.local

You should see a page showing the following information. Keep it open. You’ll need this information in the next steps.

  • Your DNS Server Address
  • Your Router’s Web Interface
  • Your AdGuard Home Web Interface

Note

  • If this page isn't ready or you see "___.___.___.___" (blank, without number) on it, it means the initialization tasks are still running. Please wait a few seconds.
  • The initialization should not take longer than 10 minutes. If you have waited more than 10 minutes, please restart the device and try again.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If you're unable to open http://yanap.local, try using a different web browser or operating system. Some systems or browsers do not support the .local domain.

WindowsmacOS & iOSAndroidLinux
  • Windows 10, Windows 11 support the .local domain by default.
  • Versions prior to Windows 10 do not support the .local domain by default.
  • macOS versions since macOS X Jaguar (version 10.2, 2002) support the .local domain by default.
  • All versions of iOS support the .local domain at the system level, though actual support may vary by app.
  • Android does not support the .local domain out of the box.

  • Most Linux distributions support .local domain, but functionality depends on your specific network configuration.

    Tip

    If you need help enabling support for the .local domain on your Linux distribution, try searching for "mDns configuration for Linux."

docs.title: Default Internet Access Flow
docs.text:
If you have never touched your DNS configuration in your LAN environment, then your situation is similar to the diagram below.

Think of DNS like the internet's address book. When you do anything online, the first step is your device asking a DNS server where to go.

Diagram 1 — Illustrative sketch of the internet access flow with default DNS   /   Drawing with Excalidraw.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

graph LR
  A[Your PC, Phone, Smart TV/Speakers/Plugs, Camera, etc.] -->|➊ send **URL** to| B[DNS Server];
  B -->|➋ reply with matching **IP** to| A;
  A -->|➌ use **IP** to connect to| C[Content / App Servers];
Diagram 2 — Flowchart of the internet access flow with default DNS

"Default" — In other words, you are using the DNS picked by your ISP to serve Their Own Interests.This can lead to the following potential1 consequences:

  • They, your ISP and the DNS service provider, have your metadata — for example, when you go online, and which websites, services, or apps you use. They can't see the full content, but even without that, the metadata alone is usually enough to reconstruct your activity: whether you were watching videos, reading posts, browsing images, or playing games.
  • Often, they sell your metadata to data brokers, ad networks, or other third parties. That's when things get more invasive. Once it's combined with other data sources, they can often figure out exactly what video you watched, which product you checked out, whose profile you viewed, what you searched — all of it. With enough data, you can be identified through profiling and social engineering.
  • Even if your ISP doesn't sell your data, there's still a risk it could be leaked or misused. This could happen through a data breach, careless employees, or government access.
  • In the worst-case scenario, if the DNS server itself is doing evil things, your online safety is seriously at risk. You could be silently redirected to phishing sites, malware, or scams without even realizing it.

These points don't cover every possible risk, but they do show some common ones.

docs.title: Internet Access Flow with DNS-Based Blocker
docs.text:
The AdGuard Home I'm using in YANAP is not the only DNS-based blocker out there. There are other FOSS options that offer similar features, such as Pi-Hole, Technitium, and others. With these DNS filters or blockers, your internet access work like the diagrams 3 and 4.

Diagram 3 — Illustrative sketch of the internet access flow with DNS-Based Blocker   /   Drawing with Excalidraw.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

graph LR
  A[Your Devices] -->|➊ send **URL** to| B[DNS Server];
  B --> |check Blocklist| D{Blocked?};
  D --> |No ➋ send **IP** to| A;
  D --> |Yes ➋ send **0.0.0.0 - Not Found** to| A;
  A --> C{Got Real IP?};
  C -->|Yes ➌ connect to| E[Content / App Servers];
  C -->|No ➌ drop into| F[BlackHole];
Diagram 4 — Flowchart of the internet access flow with DNS-Based Blocker

In this way, you regain all some control over your internet traffic.

docs.title: Can & Can't
docs.text:
A DNS-based blocker isn't a silver bullet, but it's definitely a solid start.

  • Can Block

    # most _____ on websites and apps

    • ads, affiliate
    • tracker, bug tracker, telemetry, metrics
    • Malware, Cryptojacking, scam, spam, phishing
    • social media widgets, in-page pop-ups, other annoyances
    • fake stores, fake streaming, rip-offs
    • native broadband tracker
    • badware hoster
    • malicious scripts
    • adult content
    • gambling content

    # any website you want

    # an entire online service2

  • Can't Block

    # _____ disguised as normal content3

    • video ads on Youtube, Instagram, etc.
    • sponsored posts and ads inside Facebook, TikTok, etc.

    # _____ that doesn’t access internet

    • built-in offline app ads
    • intranet-initiated attacks

    # _____ that doesn’t use your DNS

    • content with fixed IPs
    • content with fixed DNS

    # in-page or in-app scripts, like _____

    • push notifications
    • location requests

  1. Just because I use the word "potential" does not mean that I am unsure of what I am talking about. It's just that ordinary users don't have access to their data centers or logs to audit and expose their actions. ↩

  2. Blocking an entire online service means cutting off all network access related to that service provider. For example, you can block everything from Facebook, TikTok, Amazon, Xbox Live, WeChat, or Twitter. This feature covers categories such as social media, online shopping, video streaming, gambling, online gaming, and more. ↩

  3. Imagine an advertisement printed on tear-proof paper and glued between the regular pages of a dictionary. From the outside, it would be impossible to tell that the dictionary contains ads. You won't know where the ads are until you turn to the page with the ad. And even if you find one, you won't be able to tear it out with your bare hands. ↩

docs.title: Welcome to YANAP!
docs.text:
TL;DR too lang; please read    ¯\(ツ)/¯

YANAP is a combined hardware and software solution that blocks ads, tracking, phishing, and malware in home and small business LAN (Local Area Network) environments.

YANAP stands for "You Are Not A Product".

The intention behind YANAP is to offer a remarkably simple solution for those without an IT background or the spare time to deal with technical complexity, helping them to easily eliminate as many of the intrusive and harmful aspects of the Internet as possible. At its core, the project aims to empower people to reclaim their digital rights and protect their privacy, security, and identity from misuse and abuse.

docs.title: Composition of YANAP
docs.text: Drawing with Excalidraw.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Hardware - SBC (Single Board Computer)
docs.text: I'm using the Radxa Zero 3E as the hardware for YANAP. It's a budget-friendly SBC with enough power to run YANAP smoothly.

docs.title: Software - Thanks to FOSS (Free and Open Source Software)
docs.text:
YANAP is built on four key FOSS projects: DietPi, AdGuard Home, Docker & Docker Compose, and MkDocs Material, and many Contributors who maintain the Filters.

These are the real core components of YANAP. What I’ve done is simply create some lightweight scripts1 to make them self-configuring and self-maintaining, so they can better adapt to your LAN environment.

docs.title: DietPi
docs.text:
a lightweight and highly optimized Debian-based Linux operating system, designed for single-board computers (SBCs) and low-resource devices. It enables this project to run on minimal SBC hardware stably with only a few small tweaks. For you, the user, hat means you won't need to spend a lot of money.

  • Official Website, Official GitHub Repository
  • DietPi is released under the GNU General Public License v2.0 (GPLv2).
  • © 2025 DietPi Contributors

docs.title: Docker & Docker Compose
docs.text:
used in YANAP to provide a stable and isolated runtime environment for AdGuard Home and MkDocs Material, enabling easy deployment and reliable operation.

  • Docker: Official Website, Official GitHub Repository
  • Docker Compose: Official Document of Docker Compose, Official GitHub Repository
  • Docker & Docker Compose are released under Apache License 2.0.
  • © 2025 Docker Inc. All rights reserved

docs.title: AdGuard Home
docs.text:
a network-wide software that gives you control over blocking Advertisement, Tracking, Phishing, Malware, and Adult Content.

  • Official Website, Official GitHub Repository
  • AdGuard Home is released under GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPLv3).
  • © 2009–2025 Adguard Software Ltd.

docs.title: MkDocs Material
docs.text:
a modern, responsive theme for MkDocs, a static site generator. What you’re reading now was built using MkDocs Material.

  • Official Website, Official GitHub Repository
  • MkDocs Material is released under MIT License
  • © 2016–2025 Martin Donath

Acknowledgment

This project would not be possible without the incredible work of the open source community. I express my sincere gratitude not only to the specific projects used in YANAP, but also to all developers, maintainers, document writers, testers, designers, and supporters who contribute to open source software around the world.

Even the tiniest contribution counts!

I encourage everyone to give more attention to open source communities and support them in any way possible:

  • Sharing and Promoting FOSS
  • Providing Feedback and Suggestions
  • Reporting Issues or Bugs
  • Sponsoring or Donating
  • Translating Projects
  • Helping Others in Forums or Discussions
  • Creating Tutorials or How-To Guides
  • Contributing Code

  1. Once I've finished the tests and organized all the scripts and documents, I will also open source my scripts. I will provide an overview after I release the source. ↩

docs.title: Where Your Money Goes
docs.text: This project isn't about making money. I'm doing my best to be as transparent as possible with the costs and keep your price as low as I can.

docs.title: Pricing Logic
docs.text:
Here's the thinking behind the price:

  1. Cover the basics -- hardware and all the direct costs.
  2. Prepare for possible extra costs -- for example, tax-related expenses (if they come up), or the cost of acquiring, maintaining, or replacing the test units I use for development and debugging.
  3. Experiment a little -- give me room to try new ideas for improvements.
  4. Give back -- to support the FOSS that this project relies on, a portion of the money will be donated to them. (More details on how this is done will be shared after the project has been running for a while and once there's a clearer picture of actual ongoing costs.)

docs.title: A Few Notes
docs.text:
• Platform fees aren't included in the prices above. It depends on which platform you choose.
  • Prices may go up or down depending on the hardware market. I'll make adjustments as fairly as I can.

  • MicroSD cards and 3D printed cases are consumables. Their lifespan depends heavily on how and where they're used. In normal conditions, they'll usually last for a few years. But in more extreme environments (like in very hot or sunny places), they might fail much sooner - even within a few months. To give them the best chance, I've chosen endurance-grade cards and sturdy printing materials, balancing durability and cost.

    As long as you use it in the proper environment, there's no need to be overly concerned. Even if they break, the replacement costs are not too expensive.

  • Since the price is already set as close to the actual cost as possible, I'm not able to cover shipping if you ever need to return or replace something. That's one of the trade-offs for keeping things affordable.

docs.title: I Won't Run Any Ads.
docs.text:
• First, ads cost money, and that cost is passed on to you.
  • More importantly, showing ads would go directly against what YANAP is for. It wouldn't make sense to do the opposite just to fund it.

Tip

If you think YANAP is worth using, the best support you can give is simply telling someone else about it. That could be your family, a friend, someone you work or study with, or anyone who might find it useful.

docs.title: Blocking a Service
docs.text:
If you want, AdGuard Home can block an entire online service. This feature is very useful in many situations. For example:

  • Blocking social media in your office.

  • Blocking online gaming platforms when your kids have an online class.

  • When you want to reduce online shopping.

  • Blocking specific companies from snooping around in your data and information.

To do this, click Filters➊, then click Blocked services➋ to open the configuration page.

Click the image to enlarge.

On the configuration page, select the service you want to block and toggle it's switch to On➊.

After that, scroll down in this section and click the Save➋ button to apply the changes.

The service shown in the screenshot is for illustrative purposes only.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

For further precise control you can set up and manage a blocking schedule in the Pause service blocking➌ section below.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Dashboard page provides an overview of your internet requests.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Detail
docs.text:
The Query Log page shows detailed logs of all your internet requests.

Here, you can manually unblock Misblocking or block Missed Block. You’ll learn how to do both on the next page.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Parental Control
docs.text:
If needed, AdGuard Home can block adult content.

To enable this feature, click Settings➊, then click General settings➋ to open the configuration page.

Click the image to enlarge.

On the configuration page, you can activate the Options➊➋ based on your needs.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Temporarily Pause
docs.text:
If you want to temporarily pause blocking, click the dropdown arrow on the Disable protection➊ button and choose a duration.

Or, click the Disable protection➊ button directly to pause indefinitely. You'll need to click it again to manually resume protection.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Sign In
docs.text:
Click the link of Your AdGuard Home Web Interface➊ on Device Info Page to open Your AdGuard Home➋.

Then enter your Username & Password➌ to Sign In➍.

Your Account Information is printed on the paper that came with your package.

Click the image to enlarge.

Note

If you’re manually entering the IP address or URL of Your AdGuard Home Web Interface in the browser, don’t forget to include the port number :7373 at the end.

docs.title: Misblocking
docs.text:
Navigate to Query Log page. Find the URL➊ that you don’t want to block. Click the Three Dots Icon➋ to open the menu, then click Unblock➌.

The unblock takes effect after the system or app clears its DNS cache. This might take just a few seconds, or it could take several minutes depending on the system and application.

The domain shown in the screenshot is for illustrative purposes only.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Missed Block
docs.text:
Navigate to Query Log page. Find the URL➊ that you want to block. Click the Three Dots Icon➋ to open the menu, then click Block➌.

The block takes effect immediately.

The domain shown in the screenshot is for illustrative purposes only.   /   Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: ASUS
docs.text:
The set values (e.g., IP address) shown in the screenshots are for reference only. Please follow the tutorial and enter the information shown on your own YANAP page.

The interface on your router may look slightly different depending on your hardware model and firmware version, but the overall process remains the same.

Tip

Don’t worry about messing things up. You can always write down the original values in Step 3. If something goes wrong, just change them back and reboot your router. Everything will work again.

docs.title: Step 1 - Log In to Your ASUS Router
docs.text:
Click the link of Your Router's Web Interface➊ on Device Info Page to open Your Router's Settings Page➋. Enter your Username & Password➌ and click Sign In➍.

  • If you don’t know the password, check the label on your router for the default password.

  • If you’ve changed the default password but forgot it, the only option is to reset your router.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 2 - Find the Setting Page
docs.text:
Once logged in, you will see a page similar to the screenshot below, click LAN➊ from the left sidebar.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 3 - Configure Your DNS Server
docs.text:
On this screen, follow these steps:

  1. Open the DNS configuration panel:

    • click DHCP Server➊

  2. Set your own DNS server addresses:

    • enter IP Address of your DNSv4 server➋ into DNS Server 1➌

    • enter IP Address of your DNSv6 server➍ into IPv6 DNS Server➎

      (If you don’t see IPv6 DNS Server, just skip this step.)

  3. Switch Off This Option:

    • ensure Advertise router's IP in addition to user-specified DNS is set to No➏

  4. Apply the changes:

    • click Apply➐

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 4 - Reboot Your Router
docs.text: Reboot your ASUS router to make sure the changes take effect.

docs.title: Step 5 - Reconnect Your Devices<sup>1</sup>
docs.text:
To make sure everything works right away, you need to reconnect your devices to the internet.

  • If your device connects to the internet via Wi-Fi: Turn Wi-Fi Off then Turn Wi-Fi On.
  • If your device connects to the internet using an Ethernet cable: Unplug the Ethernet Cable then Plug in the Ethernet Cable.
  • If your device connects to the internet via Wi-Fi but has no option to Turn Wi-Fi off / Turn Wi-Fi On: Just restart the device.

docs.title: Done - Test & Move On
docs.text:
From now on, you should see significantly fewer ads, trackers, and pop-ups. Try visiting an ad-heavy website to check if the blocking are working.

docs.title: FRITZ!Box
docs.text:
The set values (e.g., IP address) shown in the screenshots are for reference only. Please follow the tutorial and enter the information shown on your own YANAP page.

The interface on your router may look slightly different depending on your hardware model and firmware version, but the overall process remains the same.

Tip

Don’t worry about messing things up. You can always write down the original values in Step 3. If something goes wrong, just change them back and reboot your router. Everything will work again.

docs.title: Step 1 - Log In to Your FRITZ!Box
docs.text:
Click the link of Your Router's Web Interface➊ on Device Info Page to open Your Router's Settings Page➋. Enter your Password➌ and click Log In➍.

  • If you don’t know the password, check the label on your router for the default password.

  • If you’ve changed the default password but forgot it, the only option is to reset your router.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 2 - Find the Setting Page
docs.text:
Once logged in, you will see a page similar to the screenshot below, click Internet➊ from the left sidebar.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 3 - Configure Your DNS Server
docs.text:
On this screen, follow these steps:

  1. Open the DNS configuration panel:

    • click Type of Connection➊    →    click DNS Server➋

  2. Set your own DNS server addresses:

    • activate Use other DNSv4 servers➌    →    enter IP Address of your DNSv4 server➍ into Preferred DNSv4 Server➎ and Alternative DNSv4 Server➎

    • activate Use other DNSv6 servers➏    →    enter IP Address of your DNSv6 server➐ into Preferred DNSv6 Server➑ and Alternative DNSv6 Server➑

  3. Allow backup DNS just in case:

    • activate Fallback to public DNS servers when DNS disrupted➒

    This ensures your router will use the ISP’s DNS if your YANAP server is unavailable.

  4. Apply the changes:

    • click Apply➓

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 4 - Confirm Your Configuration
docs.text:
After clicking Apply, you may or may not see the screen below. If it appears, follow the on-screen instructions. In most cases, the easiest and most user-friendly way is Confirm with FRITZ!Box button.

You need to click No telephone? Confirm with FRITZ!Box button or app to get more instructions. By default, the FRITZ!Box shows confirmation instructions for telephone only.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 5 - Final Confirmation
docs.text:
You have to confirm one more time by clicking OK.

Click the image to enlarge.

docs.title: Step 6 - Reboot Your Router
docs.text: Reboot your FRITZ!Box to make sure the changes take effect.

docs.title: Step 7 - Reconnect Your Devices<sup>1</sup>
docs.text:
To make sure everything works right away, you need to reconnect your devices to the internet.

  • If your device connects to the internet via Wi-Fi: Turn Wi-Fi Off then Turn Wi-Fi On.
  • If your device connects to the internet using an Ethernet cable: Unplug the Ethernet Cable then Plug in the Ethernet Cable.
  • If your device connects to the internet via Wi-Fi but has no option to Turn Wi-Fi off / Turn Wi-Fi On: Just restart the device.

docs.title: General Tutorial
docs.text:
Tip

  • Don’t worry about messing things up. You can always write down the original values in Step 4. If something goes wrong, just change them back and reboot your router. Everything will work again.
  • Another tip: You can refer to the tutorials from the "OK List". The interface will look different, and the steps will vary, but the logic and principles are the same.

docs.title: Step 1 - Log In to Your Router
docs.text:
Click the link of Your Router's Web Interface➊ on your Device Info Page to open the settings page of your router.

Then you will be asked to log in.

  • If you don’t know the password, check the label on your router for the default password.

  • If you’ve changed the default password but forgot it, the only option is to reset your router.

docs.title: Step 2 - Find the Setting Page
docs.text:
Find where to change DNS Server on your router's web interface.

  • If you have no idea where to find it, try searching online using this format: Your Router Model/Brand + How to change the DNS server.

docs.title: Step 3 - Configure Your DNS Server
docs.text:
At this step, do one of the following, depending on what your router allows:

  • Option 1

    If there’s a toggle or dropdown like Connect DNS server automatically / Get from ISP / Obtain DNS automatically (or similar wording),

    then switch it to Manual / No / Use the following DNS addresses (or similar wording).

  • Option 2

    If there’s no such toggle, but you see fields already filled with DNS addresses, then delete the existing addresses to clear them out.

Do this for both IPv4 and IPv6 (if IPv6 DNS settings are available).

Note Well: How do I know if IPv6 DNS setting is available or not on my router?

  • Case 1

    If you only see settings labeled IPv4 orDNSv4, and nothing about IPv6 or DNSv6, then ignore all IPv6-related steps.

  • Case 2

    If there are only two blank fields for DNS input, it likely means you can only set IPv4 DNS.

  • Case 3

    If the DNS setting fields only accept numbers (no ":" characters allowed), it means only IPv4 DNS is supported.

docs.title: Step 4 - Enter Your Own DNS Server Address
docs.text:
Now enter your own DNS Server Address shown on Device Info Page.

IPv4 DNS SettingIPv6 DNS Setting
  • Enter IP Address of your DNSv4 server➊ into the first blank field, often labeled Primary DNS, DNS Server 1 or similar wording.
  • Click Save or Apply.
  • If you're unable to save with some fields left blank, try entering the IP Address of your DNSv4 server➊ in all available fields, then click Save or Apply again.
  • Enter IP Address of your DNSv6 server➋ into all blank fields.
  • Click Save or Apply.

docs.title: Step 5 - Reboot Your Router<sup>1</sup>
docs.text: Reboot your router to make sure the changes take effect.

docs.title: Step 6 - Reconnect Your Devices<sup>2</sup>
docs.text:
To make sure everything works right away, you need to reconnect your devices to the internet.

  • If your device connects to the internet via Wi-Fi: Turn Wi-Fi Off then Turn Wi-Fi On.
  • If your device connects to the internet using an Ethernet cable: Unplug the Ethernet Cable then Plug in the Ethernet Cable.
  • If your device connects to the internet via Wi-Fi but has no option to Turn Wi-Fi off / Turn Wi-Fi On: Just restart the device.

docs.title: Long Story Short
docs.text:
In this step, you need to replace the default DNS Server Address (usually assigned by your ISP) with your own DNS Server Address displayed on your Device Info Page.

If you know how to handle it, you can skip this part.

docs.title: Short Story Long
docs.text:
I categorize router brands into two groups. One is called the "OK List", and the other is called the "Bad List". The differences are as follows:

  • For every brand on the "OK List", I’ve created a dedicated step-by-step tutorial with screenshots tailored to that brand to walk you through the process.

  • The routers on the "Bad List" have had their features heavily crippled or locked down by the ISP or manufacturer. Gaining full control over your own network on these devices is either impossible or painfully complicated.

    For these cases, I’ve prepared a more involved tutorial compared to the "OK List" routers. It’s still very doable, just requires more patience.

Find your router on one of the two lists, then follow the corresponding tutorial.

If your router is not listed on either list, follow the instructions for "Routers Not on Any List".
